strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: domain shift breaks standard conformal prediction for LLMs, and the paper provides empirical evidence of systematic under-coverage
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 16 diverse models, 272 domain pairs, clear visualization (Figure 3) showing the method adaptively improves coverage precisely where standard CP fails
Principled approach combining semantic embeddings with weighted conformal prediction is well-motivated for high-dimensional prompts where direct density ratio estimation is infeasible
Provides theoretical coverage guarantees (Theorems 1-2) with data-dependent weights, generalizing nonexchangeable CP and reducing to standard CP under exchangeability
Practically useful: simple algorithm (Algorithm 1), uses standard tools, set size increases are modest across most models
Honest discussion of limitations and clear acknowledgment of open problems (e.g., extension to open-ended tasks, principled λ selection)
weaknesses: Theoretical bounds are loose and impractical: error terms depend on TV(S^i, S) which cannot be estimated without test labels, providing formal validity but no guidance for practitioners on whether guarantees actually hold

Arbitrary design choices without ablation studies: (1) λ=1 lacks justification beyond 'natural balance' with no ablation on λ values; (2) embedding model all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is fixed without sensitivity analysis; (3) XGBoost hyperparameters applied with 'no tuning'
Limited experimental scope: only multiple-choice QA on MMLU despite acknowledging this requires task-specific changes for open-ended generation. No experiments on other UQ benchmarks
Missing comparisons: only compared against standard CP, not to other domain adaptation methods, importance reweighting variants, or test-time adaptation approaches

Density ratio estimation in high dimensions (384-D) receives limited analysis: no discussion of classifier calibration bias, variance in estimates, or empirical validation that ratios are accurately estimated

Insufficient empirical justification of key assumptions: (1) that conditional distributions P(Y|X) are similar across domains, (2) that embeddings preserve sufficient semantic structure for reweighting, (3) sensitivity analysis to embedding model choice is absent despite this appearing critical
No ablation studies on critical components: effect of λ values, different embedding models, different density ratio estimators, or different nonconformity scores beyond LAC/APS
Unequal improvements across models (Figure 1) suggest model-dependence not fully explored, and set size increases become prohibitive for high-accuracy models (Yi-34B), limiting practical utility

Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; 272 domain pairs lack multiple-testing correction; no analysis of which model properties correlate with improvement magnitude

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitation of standard CP: domain shift breaks exchangeability assumption, critical for LLM deployment

Solid theoretical framework: Theorems 4.1-4.4 provide finite-sample coverage bounds; Theorems 4.2-4.3 elegantly show what matters is score smoothness in embedding space, not raw distribution proximity
Principled methodology: semantic embeddings handle high-dimensional prompts, regularization prevents set degeneration, method naturally reduces to standard CP under exchangeability

Comprehensive experiments: systematic evaluation across 272 subject pairs and 16 diverse LLMs; consistent coverage improvements; thoughtful ablation studies; Figure 3 provides convincing evidence of adaptive rather than uniform set inflation
Clear and honest presentation: well-written with good motivation, interpretable visualizations, candid discussion of limitations in Section 7
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: evaluation restricted to single benchmark (MMLU) and single task type (multiple-choice QA); synthetic domain shifts only (different subjects); no evaluation on open-ended generation, other benchmarks, or real-world temporal shifts

Missing critical baselines: no empirical comparison with related domain-shift-aware methods, particularly Ulmer et al. (2024) which uses similar nonexchangeable CP framework; no comparison with other uncertainty quantification or domain adaptation methods

Theory-practice gap: coverage bounds in Theorem 4.1 depend on TV(S^i, S|G) terms that cannot be estimated in practice—bounds may be vacuous; Theorem 4.3's smoothness assumption unverifiable; no finite-sample complexity analysis or guidance for practitioners

Density ratio estimation concerns: even in 384-1024 dimensional embedding space, density ratio estimation is challenging; paper uses single XGBoost classifier with no analysis of when estimation fails or sensitivity to misspecification

Modest empirical improvements: while consistent, median coverage improvements are often small (e.g., ~0.85→0.90); visible increases in prediction set sizes (Figures 2, 12) reduce practical utility; no quantification of actual CP under-coverage severity

Methodological limitations: requires unlabeled target-domain prompts (transductive setting, stronger than online prediction); λ selection remains heuristic despite theoretical justification; strong dependence on embedding model quality without principled selection guidance

Incremental novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (nonexchangeable CP from Barber et al. 2023, standard density ratio estimation, semantic embeddings); main contribution is engineering these for LLMs rather than fundamental advance
Reproducibility issues: code availability URL is blank; hyperparameter choices for XGBoost appear arbitrary without justification; preprocessing exclusion of indices [1,3,5,7,9] lacks explanation

Limited ablations and analyses: no sensitivity analysis to calibration set size or target batch size; no computational overhead quantification; no investigation of failure modes or cases where score smoothness assumption fails; no cross-benchmark evaluation
